title: Gratuity and fixed-term employment under the new Codes
author: Editorial Desk
summary: What a worker should know about the gratuity rule and the fixed-term contract.
body:
The four Labour Codes came into force on 21 November 2025, and since then two questions have come up again and again in union offices and on shop floors: who gets gratuity, and what exactly is a fixed-term employee? This post explains both in plain language, using the Government's own announcement and independent legal summaries, and then sets out the concern that unions, including BMS, have raised.

## Where gratuity comes from

Gratuity is a lump-sum payment that an employer makes to a worker when employment ends after long service. It is a form of deferred reward for years of work, and for many families it is the largest single payment they receive at retirement. Until November 2025 it was governed by the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. It is now dealt with in the Code on Social Security, 2020, which brought together a number of older social security laws.

## The general rule: five years

The basic rule did not change. Under the Code, gratuity becomes payable after five years of continuous service when employment ends through superannuation, retirement, resignation, death, disablement or another event the Central Government may notify. Working journalists are an exception and qualify after three years. The five-year condition is relaxed in three situations: death, disablement, and the expiry of a fixed-term contract.

The formula also remains familiar. Gratuity is calculated as the last drawn monthly wage divided by 26, multiplied by 15, multiplied by the number of years of service. In other words, it is fifteen days' wages for each completed year. A period of service of more than six months in the last year is counted as a full year. As an illustration of the arithmetic only, a worker whose monthly wage for this purpose is Rs 30,000 and who has completed three years would receive about Rs 51,900. The actual figure depends on what counts as wages.

## What counts as wages

This is a practical point that decides many disputes. For gratuity, wages include basic pay, dearness allowance and any retaining allowance. The Code also has a rule meant to stop employers from shrinking the base by labelling most of the pay as allowances. If the components that are excluded, such as house rent allowance, overtime or conveyance, together exceed half of the total remuneration, the excess is added back when wages are calculated. Workers should therefore look at their salary structure and not only at the headline figure.

## The new element: fixed-term employees

The change that has drawn most attention concerns fixed-term employment. The Industrial Relations Code recognises fixed-term employment as a formal category. A fixed-term employee is hired directly by the employer, for a fixed period, under a written contract. The Government's announcement of 21 November 2025 says that such employees are entitled to benefits comparable to permanent employees, and that they become eligible for gratuity after one year of continuous service, instead of five years. Legal summaries explain that the amount is worked out pro rata to the period of the contract. In a one-year contract, for example, the worker would be paid gratuity for that one year.

The Code on Social Security also says that when a fixed-term contract ends, the five-year condition does not apply. Employers have to pay the gratuity within 30 days of it becoming payable, and delay attracts simple interest. Disputes go to a competent authority, and an appeal has to be filed within 60 days.

## Equal treatment of fixed-term workers

The Industrial Relations Code lays down that a fixed-term employee should get the same working conditions, hours of work, wages and allowances as a permanent employee doing similar work, together with statutory benefits in proportion to the period of service. The Government's announcement presents this as an advantage: a young worker on a contract is not left outside the social security system.

The announcement also says that all workers must be given appointment letters stating designation, wages and social security entitlements. For fixed-term workers in particular, that letter is the record of how long the contract runs, and so it matters.

## The concern that unions raise

The principle of equal treatment is not in dispute. The concern is about use. Independent analysis by PRS Legislative Research, written when the Bills were before Parliament, noted that the Code does not restrict the type of work for which fixed-term staff may be hired, and that renewal rests with the employer. PRS pointed out that this can create job insecurity and may discourage workers from raising grievances, since a worker who complains may find that the contract is not renewed. It also recorded that a parliamentary standing committee had recommended that the conditions, areas of use and minimum and maximum tenure of fixed-term employment be specified.

PRS also flagged a drafting question that remains worth watching. At one point, the Social Security Code spoke of pro-rata gratuity for fixed-term workers, while the Industrial Relations Code referred to a one-year contract. It was unclear whether a contract shorter than one year would qualify. The Government's announcement now states a one-year rule, which answers the question for the present but leaves the detail to the rules and notifications.

Union leaders fear that, without safeguards, employers could replace permanent posts with rolling short contracts. BMS has said that fixed-term contracts must not become a substitute for regular employment in core activities, and that safeguards should be written into the rules. It has also asked for the concerns it identified in the Industrial Relations Code to be addressed, as set out in its memorandum to the Labour Minister on 21 November 2025. The Government's announcement, for its part, presents the equal-benefits provision as the safeguard for fixed-term workers.

## What to watch in the rules

- Whether the rules, central and State, limit fixed-term hiring in core or perennial work.
- How successive renewals are treated when a worker is employed again and again for short periods.
- What ceiling on the amount of gratuity is notified, since the Code leaves that to the Government.
- Whether the facility of appointment letters is checked by inspectors, who are now described as facilitators first.

## A practical guide for workers

Documents decide disputes about service and gratuity. A worker should therefore:

- Insist on an appointment letter and read the contract period and the terms of renewal.
- Keep copies of wage slips, bank statements showing salary credits, and any extension letters.
- Note the date of joining and the date of each change of status, since continuous service is what counts.
- Check how wages are shown, because the 50 per cent rule works on the salary structure.
- If gratuity is not paid within 30 days of becoming due, ask in writing, and keep a copy; delay carries interest and the competent authority can be approached.

## The way ahead

Gratuity and fixed-term employment show in a small way how the Codes work: the text gives a right, and the rules and their enforcement decide how much of it a worker receives. The new one-year rule for fixed-term staff is a gain for those who would earlier have received nothing. Whether it becomes a true protection depends on whether fixed-term hiring stays a tool for genuine short-term needs and does not become a way to avoid permanent jobs. That is the point that BMS and other unions will keep watching as the rules are finalised.
